title: From classical to quantum gravity
one_line_summary: A guided tour of candidate routes beyond classical GR: compact extra dimensions and the Planck scale, the classical Nambu-Goto string reduced to a wave equation by gauge choices, cosmic strings as topological defects, Wheeler-style superspace, loop quantum gravity's quantized tetrahedron, anti-de Sitter spacetime and its boundary, closing with the Lambda-CDM picture of our Universe.
role_in_book: The penultimate chapter looks outward from the classical theory built over the whole book. It picks up the extra-dimension and gauge-field thread of the previous (Kaluza-Klein) chapter and the effective-field-theory view of gravity as non-renormalizable, then shows how tools the reader already owns (action principles, induced metrics from Appendix D, reparametrization freedom from Chapters 8-9, phase transitions from Chapter 41, maximally symmetric spacetimes from Chapters 15-19) can be pointed at open research questions. It is deliberately a survey that ends in humility: each approach is shown to be promising but untested, and the ending sets up the final chapter on the Big Bang singularity.

assumed_background.topic: Kaluza-Klein unification via a fifth compact dimension
Gravity as a non-renormalizable effective field theory; graviton scattering
Relativistic point-particle action and reparametrization of world lines
Induced metric on an embedded surface
Euler-Lagrange equations for field Lagrangian densities and field momenta
Spontaneous symmetry breaking, early-Universe phase transitions and inflation
de Sitter spacetime, constant-curvature and maximally symmetric spaces
Killing vectors and conserved quantities along geodesics
FRW cosmology, density parameters, matter and radiation scaling, Einstein-de Sitter model
Particle in a box, Heisenberg uncertainty, angular momentum commutators and eigenvalues j(j+1)
Feynman path integral as a sum over histories
Dimensional analysis with G, c and hbar
Vector cross and triple products, projection onto a unit vector

learning_objectives: Reader can solve the Schrodinger equation on a strip with one compact direction and explain why extra dimensions of small radius a only show up at energies of order hbar^2/(2 m a^2).
Reader can build the Planck length, time and mass from G, c and hbar and convert the Planck length into an energy scale of about 10^19 GeV, comparing it with LHC and cosmic-ray energies.

Reader can argue from Gauss's law that gravity falls off as 1/r^(d-1) in d spatial dimensions and relate the higher-dimensional coupling G^(D) to the measured G through the volume of the compact dimensions.
Reader can explain why replacing point vertices with string world sheets softens the short-distance divergences of quantum field theory.
Reader can write the Nambu-Goto action as tension times world-sheet area using the induced metric, identify the world-sheet momenta and state the resulting equations of motion.
Reader can use static gauge and a velocity-perpendicular, energy-weighted choice of sigma to reduce the string equation of motion to a one-dimensional wave equation.

Reader can describe how domain walls and vortices arise when a symmetry-breaking phase transition picks different vacua in different regions, and how stacking vortices yields a cosmic string that lenses light into double images.
Reader can describe superspace as the space of all 3-geometries with an amplitude on each, and state the role of the Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation.

Reader can reproduce the heuristic that localizing a particle below the Planck length would form a black hole, and explain how angular-momentum-like commutators for tetrahedron face-area vectors quantize area and volume in loop quantum gravity.
Reader can write the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter hyperboloid embeddings, contrast their signatures, topologies and curvature signs, and pass between them with alpha^2 -> -alpha^2.

Reader can derive the conformal form of the AdS3 line element, locate the timelike boundary at psi = pi/2 (or w = 0 in Poincare coordinates), and show that massive particles turn back at w = b while light reaches the boundary.
Reader can summarize the Lambda-CDM timeline and the measured density fractions, and list its unsolved problems (dark matter identity, dark energy, inflation, lithium-7, Hubble tension).

teaching_approach.summary: A survey chapter that reuses the book's own toolkit rather than importing new formalism. Each research programme is presented through one concrete, solvable calculation (a quantum particle on a cylinder, dimensional analysis for Planck units, a string action reduced to a wave equation, a tetrahedron treated as a set of angular momenta, a particle bouncing off the AdS boundary), wrapped in candid commentary about what is untested. The string section is the only sustained derivation and deliberately mirrors the point-particle action line by line; the later sections become progressively more descriptive, and the chapter ends by stepping back from speculation to the observationally anchored Lambda-CDM model.
narrative_arc: Motivating problem: three of the four interactions are unified as quantum gauge theories, but gravity resists; start from the previous chapter's extra-dimension idea
Quick side route (Coleman footnote): a tiny bit of quantum mechanics already gives gravitational redshift by rescaling time with the potential
Why hidden dimensions stay hidden: particle in a well with one compactified direction has new levels only at energies set by the tiny radius
Where the new physics lives: Planck units from dimensional analysis, the 10^19 GeV gap to accelerators
Consequence for gravity: Newton-Poisson law in D dimensions, force law 1/r^(d-1), G equals G^(5) divided by the compact circumference
String theory motivated by the divergence problem: point vertices versus smooth trouser-shaped world sheets; D-branes and closed strings
Formalism by analogy: point-particle length action -> world-sheet area action via the induced metric (Nambu-Goto)
Simplify by gauge choice: static gauge, transverse velocity, and a sigma parametrization that turns the equations into a wave equation; graviton as closed-string mode
Strings in relativity more broadly: supersymmetry and dark matter, M-theory's lack of falsifiable predictions, cosmic strings as vortex lines from early-Universe symmetry breaking, lensing signature
A conservative alternative: superspace of 3-geometries, Feynman phases and the Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation, Planck-scale fuzziness of the metric
A radical alternative: loop quantum gravity, motivated by the mini-black-hole argument and built by quantizing tetrahedron area vectors like angular momentum

A geometric ingredient: de Sitter and anti-de Sitter hyperboloids, unrolling AdS, conformal coordinates reveal a boundary, Poincare coordinates show massive particles cannot reach it; holography and AdS/CFT named
Reality check: the Lambda-CDM timeline, measured Omega values, successes and open problems; hand-off to the Big Bang chapter
signature_moves: Every speculative programme is anchored by one small calculation a reader can actually do with standard undergraduate tools
The string is built by strict analogy with the relativistic particle: mass becomes tension, proper length becomes world-sheet area, affine reparametrization becomes gauge choice
Gauge fixing is presented as the same trick as choosing a convenient world-line parameter earlier in the book, now exercised twice (tau and sigma)
Quantum geometry is made concrete by mapping tetrahedron face-area vectors onto angular momentum operators, so familiar results (j(j+1) spectra, incompatible components) carry over
de Sitter and anti-de Sitter are handled as a matched pair differing only by a sign flip of alpha^2 and an extra timelike embedding direction
The AdS boundary is probed operationally by firing photons and massive particles at it and reading off an effective Newtonian potential
Frequent candid caveats and humour (Coleman's warning about doing a thesis in GR, 'Or might not!') keep the speculative status of each theory explicit

sections.title: Chapter opening: gravity outside the Standard Model
sections.summary: Recalls that electromagnetism, the weak and the strong forces are combined in the Standard Model as quantum gauge theories while gravity is the holdout, and announces a tour of attempts to place gravity in the quantum world starting from extra dimensions. Two margin notes set the tone: gravity can be kept as a low-energy effective theory despite non-renormalizability, and a Coleman argument shows that inserting a gravitational potential into the quantum time-evolution operator is equivalent to rescaling time, giving gravitational redshift at once.
concepts: gravitational redshift from quantum time evolution
key_moves: Gravity singled out as the one interaction not incorporated on the same footing as the others
Effective-field caveat: non-renormalizable gravity is fine below a cutoff
Coleman shortcut: H -> H(1+V) is the same as t -> (1+V)t, so clocks lower in the potential run slow

sections.title: Extra dimensions
sections.summary: Asks why extra spatial dimensions, if they exist, have not been noticed. A particle in a box with one compactified direction shows that the new energy levels scale with the inverse square of the compact radius, so a tiny radius pushes them out of reach. Planck's natural units are built by dimensional analysis, giving lengths of 10^-35 m and energies of 10^19 GeV far beyond the LHC. The Poisson equation is then generalized to D spacetime dimensions: the force law steepens to 1/r^(d-1), and for a compact fifth dimension the measured G is the five-dimensional coupling diluted by the compact circumference, generalizing to G^(D)/G equal to the compact volume.
concepts: gravitational force law in d spatial dimensions
key_moves: Separable solution on a strip with periodic y gives E_nl with an additive (l/a)^2 term; l = 0 reproduces the ordinary levels
Small compact radius a << L means first new level sits at about hbar^2/(2 m a^2)
Solve G, c, hbar for a length, time and mass scale
Natural units: length inverse to energy, so probing 10^-35 m needs 10^19 GeV
Poisson equation with dimension-dependent G^(D); Gauss-law scaling of force with r
Integrate density over the compact circle: rho^(5) = rho^(4)/(2 pi a), so G = G^(5)/(2 pi a)

sections.title: String theory
sections.summary: Introduces strings as structureless one-dimensional fundamental objects whose vibrations are the particles; strings may be open (with free ends or ends fixed on D-branes) or closed. The main selling point is that interactions are smeared over a smooth world sheet rather than concentrated at a vertex, easing the divergences of perturbative quantum field theory, and a closed string naturally contains a massless spin-2 mode. The classical theory is then built by analogy with the relativistic particle: a world sheet X^mu(tau, sigma), its induced 2x2 metric, and the Nambu-Goto action equal to minus the tension times the world-sheet area, from which world-sheet momenta and equations of motion follow.
concepts: induced metric on the world sheet
key_moves: Feynman vertex at a point versus smooth pair-of-pants world sheet: no single interaction point
Recall point-particle action -m times proper length, parametrized by tau
Promote world line to world sheet with two parameters tau and sigma
Pull back eta_{mu nu} with the embedding to get gamma_{alpha beta} built from Xdot^2, Xdot.X', X'^2
Action proportional to area integral of sqrt(-gamma), with tension T0 replacing mass
Treat X^mu as fields on the (tau, sigma) plane; momenta P^tau_mu and P^sigma_mu; conservation-law form of the equations of motion

sections.title: Parametrizing the string
sections.summary: Exploits the reparametrization freedom of the world sheet to simplify the equations. Static gauge sets tau equal to coordinate time, so constant-tau slices are snapshots of the string. Measuring position along the string by arc length s leads to the transverse velocity, the component of the string's velocity perpendicular to its tangent, and the action becomes a tension-weighted integral of the relativistic factor sqrt(1 - v_perp^2) along the string. Choosing sigma so that velocity is perpendicular to the string and so that ds/dsigma equals sqrt(1 - v_perp^2) collapses the equations of motion into the one-dimensional wave equation, whose modes, once quantized, would be particles including the graviton.
key_moves: Static gauge: tau = t, so dX^mu/dtau = (1, dX/dt) and dX^mu/dsigma = (0, dX/dsigma)
Arc length s makes dX/ds a unit tangent; project velocity perpendicular to it
Show the square-root argument equals (ds/dsigma)^2 (1 - v_perp^2)
Action rewritten as -T0 times integral of ds sqrt(1 - v_perp^2): only transverse motion is physical
Impose velocity orthogonal to tangent, then fix sigma by (ds/dsigma)(1 - v_perp^2)^(-1/2) = 1
Result: d^2X/dt^2 = d^2X/dsigma^2

sections.title: Strings in relativity
sections.summary: Surveys where strings meet gravitation. Superstrings are Planck-sized supersymmetric strings; supersymmetry pairs every boson with a fermion partner, and such partners are one candidate for dark matter, which is inferred only gravitationally. M-theory generalizes superstrings to branes but has not produced falsifiable predictions. Separately, cosmic strings are macroscopic defects formed in early-Universe phase transitions: a real scalar field with a double-well potential can form domain walls between regions in opposite vacua, and a complex field with a Mexican-hat potential forms vortices whose phase winds around a singular core; stacking vortex cores gives a line, the cosmic string, whose tension would split distant sources into double images by lensing. Black holes as strings is mentioned as a speculative link.
concepts: gravitational lensing by a cosmic string
key_moves: Supersymmetry operator swaps boson and fermion states; superpartner naming (photino, squark)
Dark matter as possibly supersymmetric partners suppressed from interacting with ordinary matter
Honest verdict: M-theory lacks testable predictions; Planck-scale force-law changes are unmeasurable
Double-well cooling -> domains in +phi0 and -phi0 -> wall where the field interpolates
Complex field: ring of degenerate minima; phase winding around a point forces a singular core
Stack 2D vortices along a third direction to make a line defect = cosmic string
Observable: conical space around the string produces double images

sections.title: Superspace
sections.summary: Presents the view that a rigid spacetime is a classical approximation. Spacetime is sliced into spacelike 3-geometries; quantum mechanics requires enlarging this set to superspace, containing every possible 3-geometry with an amplitude on each. In a sum-over-histories picture each amplitude carries a phase set by the classical action, so the dynamics is governed by how surfaces of constant action propagate through superspace, described by the Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation, which carries the same content as the Einstein field equation. Planck-scale metric fluctuations spread appreciable amplitude over many 3-geometries, limiting how far a smooth spacetime picture can be trusted. The approach is praised as conservative because it needs only the metric field.
key_moves: Deconstruct spacetime into stackable spacelike 3-surfaces
Quantum version: superposition over all 3-geometries with amplitudes psi(3-geometry)
Phase of each contribution is exp(iS/hbar); constructive interference where actions agree
Wavefronts of constant S in superspace obey the Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation
Planck-scale fluctuations give many 3-geometries appreciable amplitude, so classical spacetime is only approximate

sections.title: Loop quantum gravity
sections.summary: Motivates quantizing geometry itself. A heuristic shows that squeezing a particle into a region of size L gives it energy hbar c/L, whose horizon radius reaches L exactly at the Planck length, so sub-Planckian structure is hidden. Borrowing the logic that commutation relations cause quantization, a tetrahedron is described by four face-normal vectors whose magnitudes are face areas and which sum to zero; promoting them to operators with angular-momentum commutators scaled by a Planck-sized length squared makes each face area take discrete values proportional to sqrt(j(j+1)) and makes the orientation of faces uncertain. Volume commutes with closure, so tetrahedra carry discrete quanta of volume. Networks of such cells reduce to graphs whose closed paths are the loops. The section ends by stressing that LQG has no established semiclassical limit and no new predictions.
key_moves: Uncertainty: momentum at least hbar/L; ultra-relativistic energy at least hbar c/L
Set horizon radius G E/c^4 equal to L: L = Planck length
Tetrahedron encoded by four area vectors summing to zero; V^2 = (2/9) L1 x L2 . L3
Postulate [L_a^i, L_b^j] = i delta_ab l0^2 epsilon^{ijk} L_a^k
Carry over angular momentum results: area eigenvalues l0^2 sqrt(j(j+1)); only one Cartesian component sharp
Joint eigenstates |j1 j2 j3 j4 v> give discrete volume
Mesh of cells -> graph; loops are closed paths through nodes

sections.title: Anti-de Sitter spacetime
sections.summary: Motivated by the quantum-mechanical particle in a box, looks for a spacetime that confines gravity. de Sitter spacetime is recalled as a hyperboloid in five-dimensional Minkowski space with positive constant curvature and topology R x S^3. Anti-de Sitter spacetime is the negative-curvature partner, a hyperboloid in a flat space with two timelike directions, topology S^1 x R^3, and closed timelike curves that are removed by unrolling the time circle. Global coordinates for AdS3 and a conformal rescaling show that the radial coordinate only reaches the equator, revealing a timelike boundary; Poincare coordinates show the boundary as flat Minkowski space of one lower dimension. Light reaches the boundary in finite coordinate time, but massive particles feel an effective repulsive potential and turn back, hinting at how bulk energy maps to a boundary scale, the germ of holography and AdS/CFT.
key_moves: dS: one-sheeted hyperboloid of radius alpha in (4+1)-dimensional Minkowski space; induced metric by eliminating the fifth coordinate
Sphere <-> de Sitter via T^2 -> -T^2; maximal symmetry
AdS: the analogous quadric in (3+2)-dimensional flat space with a second timelike axis U and negative right-hand side; dS <-> AdS via alpha^2 -> -alpha^2
Time is a circle in the (T,U) plane: closed timelike loops; unroll to get R^4
AdS3 global coordinates give -(1+r^2)dt^2 + dr^2/(1+r^2) + r^2 dtheta^2
r = tan psi: conformal factor 1/cos^2 psi; psi only reaches pi/2 so there is a boundary
Poincare coordinates: constant-w slices are Minkowski; boundary at w = 0
Null ray returns in coordinate time 2 w0; massive geodesic has effective potential (b/w)^2 and turns at w = b

sections.title: Our current best guess
sections.summary: Steps back to observational cosmology. COBE, WMAP and Planck measurements of the microwave background support the Lambda-CDM model: a flat Universe with about 5 per cent baryons, 26 per cent cold dark matter and 69 per cent dark energy, accelerating today. A timeline runs from inflation near 10^-32 s through hadron formation, baryon-antibaryon annihilation and baryogenesis, nucleosynthesis, recombination at 380,000 years, matter domination and dark-energy domination from about 5 Gyr ago, to an age of 13.80 Gyr. Agreement of Omega values from CMB acoustic peaks and deuterium abundance is the main reason for confidence, while lithium-7, baryogenesis, Hubble tension, the origin of inflation, and the nature of dark matter and dark energy remain open. The chapter closes by committing to the Big-Bang singularity as a robust feature, previewing the final chapter.
key_moves: CMB blackbody at 2.725 K with 10^-5 anisotropies, mapped by successive satellites
Unpack Lambda (accelerating expansion from Type Ia supernovae) and CDM (galaxy halos, rotation curves)
Budget: Omega_0 ~ 1 = 0.05 baryons + 0.26 CDM + 0.69 Lambda
Zel'dovich: naive vacuum energy overshoots by about fifty orders of magnitude
Chronological history of the Universe with key epochs
Cross-check between CMB and deuterium as evidence; list of unresolved tensions
Big-Bang singularity as the anchor for the final chapter

concepts.name: Standard Model of particle physics
concepts.definition: The quantum gauge field theory with gauge group SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1) that describes the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions of quarks, leptons and the Higgs field; gravity is not included.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the opening as the great unification success of twentieth-century physics, setting up gravity as the one interaction left over.
concepts.notes: The gauge group is not given in the chapter.

concepts.name: effective field theory of gravity
aliases: gravity as a low-energy effective theory
concepts.definition: The view that general relativity, although non-renormalizable, can be quantized and used reliably for processes at energies well below a cutoff (roughly the Planck energy), above which an unknown more fundamental theory must take over.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 1 recalls the previous chapter's effective-field stance to explain in what sense gravity can and cannot be fitted into the Standard Model framework.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift from quantum time evolution
concepts.definition: In a weak uniform field the rest-energy Hamiltonian acquires a potential term proportional to itself, H -> H(1+V) with V = gh (c = 1); since the evolution operator depends on the product Ht, this is equivalent to replacing t by (1+V)t, so clocks at lower potential tick more slowly.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered in margin note 2 as a quick warm-up before the complicated material, crediting an argument of Sidney Coleman.
formulas: \hat U = e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar} \to e^{-i\hat H(1+V)t/\hbar}
concepts.notes: Uses H = p^0 = m for a particle at rest in units with c = 1.

concepts.name: compactified extra dimension
concepts.definition: A spatial direction that is periodic with a small period, e.g. identifying y with y + 2 pi a, so that space locally looks like ordinary space times a small circle (or a small compact manifold); physics is unchanged at scales much larger than a.
concepts.how_introduced: Continues the Kaluza-Klein idea of the previous chapter; made concrete by turning a two-dimensional square well into a strip rolled into a cylinder of circumference 2 pi a.

concepts.name: Kaluza-Klein tower of energy levels
concepts.definition: For a quantum particle able to move around a compact circle of radius a, momentum around the circle is quantized in units of hbar/a, adding a ladder of energies proportional to l^2 hbar^2/(2 m a^2); the l = 0 states reproduce lower-dimensional physics and the first new state lies at an energy set by the tiny radius.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.1 solves the Schrodinger equation on the rolled-up well and reads off which levels are new.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name Kaluza-Klein tower.

concepts.name: Planck units
concepts.definition: The unique length, time and mass built from G, c and hbar: l_P = sqrt(G hbar/c^3) ~ 1.6e-35 m, t_P = sqrt(G hbar/c^5) ~ 5.4e-44 s, m_P = sqrt(hbar c/G) ~ 2.2e-8 kg; they mark where quantum effects and gravity are expected to be simultaneously important.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical framing (Descartes' wish for natural units, Planck's realization) followed by Example 49.2, which inverts the dimensional relations of the three constants.
concepts.notes: The printed dimensional relation for G in eqn 49.5 is missing a power of length (see gaps).

concepts.name: Planck energy
concepts.definition: E_P = m_P c^2 ~ 1.22e19 GeV, the energy needed to probe distances of order the Planck length; it exceeds LHC beam energies by about fifteen orders of magnitude and the most energetic cosmic rays by seven or eight.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in natural units by noting length is inverse to energy, with margin notes giving the direct m_P c^2 calculation and comparisons with the LHC and cosmic rays.

concepts.name: gravitational force law in d spatial dimensions
concepts.definition: With d spatial dimensions Newtonian gravity obeys a Poisson equation with a dimension-dependent coupling G^(D) and a d-dimensional mass density; Gauss's law spreads flux over a (d-1)-sphere, so the force falls off as 1/r^(d-1).
concepts.how_introduced: Generalizes the familiar Poisson equation by asking what extra dimensions would do to gravity, then uses dimensional reasoning to get the force law.
concepts.notes: The book says density is mass divided by the 'number of spatial dimensions'; it means mass per unit d-dimensional volume.

concepts.name: relation between higher-dimensional and observed gravitational constants
aliases: dilution of gravity by compact volume
concepts.definition: If gravity lives in D dimensions with D-4 of them compact, an observer at distances much larger than the compactification scale measures G = G^(D)/V_c, where V_c ~ l_c^(D-4) is the volume of the compact space; for one circle of radius a, G = G^(5)/(2 pi a).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.3 averages a five-dimensional density over the compact circle to reproduce the four-dimensional Poisson equation, then generalizes.
prerequisites: gravitational force law in d spatial dimensions
concepts.notes: This is the mechanism behind large-extra-dimension models in which the true gravity scale is much lower than the four-dimensional Planck scale; the book does not pursue that.

concepts.name: higher-dimensional Planck length
concepts.definition: The length built from hbar, c and the D-dimensional coupling G^(D): (l_P^(D))^(D-2) = hbar G^(D)/c^3 = l_P^2 G^(D)/G.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a margin note as a dimensional-analysis result, left as Exercise 49.3.
prerequisites: relation between higher-dimensional and observed gravitational constants

concepts.name: string (fundamental)
concepts.definition: A one-dimensional extended object with no internal parts, taken as fundamental in string theory; the different vibrational modes of a string appear as different particle species.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the replacement for point particles in quantum field theory, motivated by extra dimensions and by the divergence problem.

concepts.name: open and closed strings
concepts.definition: An open string has two endpoints (free, or attached to branes); a closed string is a loop. Their world sheets are respectively a ribbon-like strip and a tube.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the forms strings can take; shown as the two world sheets in Fig. 49.4.

concepts.name: D-brane
concepts.definition: An extended object of some spatial dimension p on which the endpoints of open strings are constrained to lie; the D refers to Dirichlet boundary conditions fixing the endpoint coordinates transverse to the brane.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the objects on which fixed string ends terminate, with Fig. 49.2 showing an arc of string with both ends on a 2-brane, and a margin note on Dirichlet.
concepts.notes: The margin note writes the Dirichlet condition as dX^i/dtau = 0 at the ends, i.e. fixed transverse endpoint positions.

concepts.name: ultraviolet divergences and renormalization
concepts.definition: In perturbative quantum field theory, interactions at a single spacetime point make loop integrals diverge at short distances; renormalization absorbs these into redefined parameters, which works for the Standard Model but not for perturbative quantum gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.4 contrasts a point Feynman vertex with a smooth string junction to explain why strings improve short-distance behaviour.

concepts.name: world sheet
concepts.definition: The two-dimensional surface X^mu(tau, sigma) swept out in spacetime by a moving string, the string analogue of a particle's world line; tau is time-like and sigma labels position along the string.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by direct analogy with a world line: one parameter becomes two.

concepts.name: induced metric on the world sheet
concepts.definition: The 2x2 metric gamma_{alpha beta} = eta_{mu nu} dX^mu/dxi^alpha dX^nu/dxi^beta that the ambient spacetime metric induces on the world sheet; in (tau, sigma) coordinates its entries are Xdot^2, Xdot.X' and X'^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by the embedding routine of Appendix D, then written as an explicit matrix using dot and prime notation.
concepts.notes: The text calls the ambient space Euclidean but uses the Minkowski metric eta; the target space is Minkowski spacetime.

concepts.name: Nambu-Goto action
concepts.definition: The action for a relativistic string equal to minus the string tension times the proper area of its world sheet, S = -T0 integral dtau dsigma sqrt(-gamma), with gamma the determinant of the induced metric; it is invariant under reparametrizations of (tau, sigma).
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed by analogy: a particle's action is -m times proper length of the world line, so a string's is -T0 times proper area of the world sheet.
prerequisites: induced metric on the world sheet
formulas: S = -T_0\int d\tau\, d\sigma\, \sqrt{(\dot X\cdot X')^2 - \dot X^2 X'^2}
concepts.notes: Printed eqns 49.18-49.19 drop the dot on the first X.

concepts.name: string tension
concepts.definition: The constant T0 (energy per unit length, equivalently force) multiplying world-sheet area in the Nambu-Goto action; it plays the role that rest mass plays for a point particle.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the constant of proportionality between area and action.

concepts.name: relativistic point-particle action
concepts.definition: S = -m integral dtau sqrt(-g_{mu nu} dx^mu/dtau dx^nu/dtau), proportional to the proper time along the world line; extremizing it gives geodesic motion and conserved momentum for a free particle.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from earlier chapters as the template from which the string action is built.

concepts.name: world-sheet momentum currents
concepts.definition: The derivatives of the string Lagrangian density with respect to Xdot^mu and X'^mu; the equations of motion say their combined divergence on the world sheet vanishes, a conservation-law form of the dynamics.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.5 treats X^mu as fields on the (tau, sigma) plane and applies the field Euler-Lagrange equation recalled in margin note 11.

concepts.name: gauge choice (world-sheet reparametrization)
concepts.definition: Because the Nambu-Goto action does not depend on how the world sheet is labelled, one may choose tau and sigma to simplify the equations; each such choice is a gauge, and physical results cannot depend on it.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the string version of choosing a convenient affine parameter for world lines in Chapters 8-9.
concepts.notes: Reparametrization invariance is Exercise 49.2.

concepts.name: static gauge
concepts.definition: The world-sheet gauge tau = t, so each constant-tau curve is the string as seen by a given observer at a fixed coordinate time.
concepts.how_introduced: The first and most direct gauge choice, pictured in Fig. 49.5 as a constant-t plane cutting the world sheet.

concepts.name: transverse velocity of a string
concepts.definition: The part of the velocity of a string point perpendicular to the string's unit tangent dX/ds; motion along the string is not physically meaningful, and the action depends only on v_perp.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.6 defines arc length, builds the unit tangent, projects out the tangential part of the velocity, and shows the Lagrangian becomes (ds/dsigma) sqrt(1 - v_perp^2).
concepts.notes: Makes the analogy with the particle Lagrangian -m sqrt(1 - v^2) explicit.

concepts.name: string wave equation
concepts.definition: In static gauge with sigma chosen so velocity is normal to the string and ds/dsigma = sqrt(1 - v_perp^2), the Nambu-Goto equations reduce to d^2X/dt^2 = d^2X/dsigma^2, supplemented by the gauge constraints; solutions are superpositions of left- and right-moving waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.7 shows the successive simplifications, concluding that the string supports wavelike excitations that would become particles after quantization.
concepts.notes: The book omits the second constraint (dX/dt)^2 + (dX/dsigma)^2 = 1 that accompanies this gauge.

concepts.name: graviton
concepts.definition: The quantum of the gravitational field, a massless spin-2 particle; in string theory it appears automatically as a vibrational state of the closed string.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 8 and the end of Section 49.3 mention it as the reason string theory is said to contain gravity.

concepts.name: superstring
concepts.definition: A string theory incorporating supersymmetry, with strings of roughly Planck-length size, whose spectrum contains both bosons and fermions.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the most prominent appearance of strings in relativity.

concepts.name: supersymmetry
concepts.definition: A proposed symmetry whose generator Q turns bosonic states into fermionic ones and vice versa, so each particle has a superpartner of opposite statistics; exact supersymmetry would give partners equal masses, which experiments rule out, so it must be broken if it exists.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.8 introduces it as one proposed explanation of dark matter, with naming rules (fermionic partners end in -ino, bosonic partners get an s- prefix).
concepts.notes: The book states partners have the same mass without noting that the symmetry must be broken; the standard photon partner is the photino.

concepts.name: dark matter
concepts.definition: Non-luminous, non-baryonic matter detected so far only through gravity (galaxy rotation curves, halos, cosmological structure); cold means its particles move slowly compared with c, so it clumps into galaxy halos. It makes up about 26 per cent of the cosmic energy budget.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Example 49.8 as a problem that supersymmetry might solve, then revisited quantitatively in Section 49.8 as the CDM of Lambda-CDM.

concepts.name: M-theory
concepts.definition: A proposed framework generalizing superstring theories to include higher-dimensional membranes (branes), hoped to unify all four interactions; it has not yet produced falsifiable experimental predictions.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned after superstrings with an explicit caveat about testability.
concepts.notes: The book's gloss that the M stands for the number of brane dimensions m is not standard; the letter has no agreed meaning.

concepts.name: spontaneous symmetry breaking
concepts.definition: When a system's potential is symmetric but its lowest-energy states are not, the system settles into one of several equivalent vacua, hiding the symmetry; in the early Universe this happens as the potential changes shape on cooling.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 41 via the change from a single-well to a double-well potential in Fig. 49.6.

concepts.name: domain wall
concepts.definition: A topological defect of a real scalar field with two degenerate vacua: a region where the field interpolates smoothly between +phi0 on one side and -phi0 on the other, costing gradient and potential energy and unable to relax away without flipping a whole domain.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.9 notes that during a phase transition different regions can choose different minima, and Fig. 49.7 plots the field across the boundary between them.
concepts.notes: The text calls it one-dimensional because the profile is along one coordinate; in 3D space a wall is a two-dimensional sheet.

concepts.name: Mexican-hat potential
aliases: broken-symmetry potential for a complex field
concepts.definition: A potential for a complex scalar field depending only on |psi| with a local maximum at zero and a circle of degenerate minima at |psi| = |psi0|; choosing a ground state means choosing a phase theta0.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictured in Fig. 49.8 via the analogy of the punt in the bottom of a wine bottle.

concepts.name: vortex (topological defect)
concepts.definition: A configuration of a complex field in which the phase theta winds by a multiple of 2 pi around a point (in 2D); continuity forces the field magnitude to vanish at the core, where the phase gradient diverges.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the simplest way the complex field can occupy different minima in different places. Fig. 49.9 draws the phase as arrows pointing radially outward from a central point, so the arrow turns once as you circle the centre. The book notes that the phase gradient blows up at the core.
concepts.notes: The winding-number formula is standard but is not written in the chapter.

concepts.name: cosmic string
concepts.definition: A hypothetical line-like topological defect formed in an early-Universe symmetry-breaking transition and stretched to astronomical length by expansion; it carries tension and mass per unit length, leaving flat space around it with a deficit angle, so it would produce double images of background sources.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by stacking two-dimensional vortices so their cores line up along a curve; its gravitational signature is lensing.
concepts.notes: Unrelated to fundamental strings except in name; Exercises 49.7-49.8 derive the conical exterior metric.

concepts.name: gravitational lensing by a cosmic string
concepts.definition: Space around a straight cosmic string is locally flat but has a missing wedge of angle, so light from a source behind the string reaches the observer along two straight paths on either side, giving two identical undistorted images.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the observable consequence of string tension; the deficit-angle geometry is made quantitative in Exercise 49.8.
concepts.notes: Deficit angle 8 pi G mu/c^2 for mass per length mu is standard but not quoted.

concepts.name: superspace (space of 3-geometries)
concepts.definition: The configuration space of quantum geometrodynamics: the set of all possible spatial 3-geometries, on each of which the quantum state assigns an amplitude; classical spacetime corresponds to a single sequence of 3-geometries through it.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by slicing spacetime into 3-surfaces and then enlarging the collection to all possible slices to accommodate quantum probability.
concepts.notes: Not the same as the supersymmetric superspace of particle physics, a name clash worth flagging.

concepts.name: 3+1 slicing of spacetime
concepts.definition: Decomposing a spacetime into a one-parameter family of spacelike 3-surfaces, each with an induced 3-metric, stacked so as to rebuild the 4-geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: The first step in constructing superspace, described without formalism.

concepts.name: sum over histories
concepts.definition: Quantum amplitudes are sums of exp(iS/hbar) over all possible histories connecting initial and final configurations, with S the classical action of each history; classical behaviour emerges where the phases add constructively.
concepts.how_introduced: Recapped in margin note 17 and applied in Example 49.10 with configurations of 3-space in place of particle paths.

concepts.name: Hamilton-Jacobi equation
concepts.definition: The formulation of classical mechanics in terms of Hamilton's principal function S, satisfying H + dS/dt = 0 with momenta given by gradients of S; its wavefronts of constant S are the classical limit of Schrodinger wave phases.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in margin note 18 to explain the kinship between classical action wavefronts and quantum phases.

concepts.name: Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation
concepts.definition: The Hamilton-Jacobi form of general relativity: a functional differential equation for the action S[gamma_ij] of 3-geometries, quadratic in dS/dgamma_ij with the DeWitt supermetric plus the 3-curvature term; together with the momentum constraint it encodes the Einstein field equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 49.10 presents it as the rule for how wavefronts of constant action move through superspace.
concepts.notes: Its quantum version is the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, not named in the book. Units and sign normalizations vary between references.

concepts.name: Planck-scale metric fluctuations
concepts.definition: The expectation that the metric field, like any quantum field, has zero-point fluctuations that become order-unity at the Planck length, so no single smooth geometry describes space at that scale.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Section 49.5 as the reason superspace amplitudes spread over many 3-geometries.

concepts.name: loop quantum gravity
concepts.definition: A non-perturbative approach that quantizes spatial geometry directly, finding discrete spectra for area and volume at the Planck scale; quantum states of geometry are labelled by graphs (spin networks) whose links carry area quanta and whose nodes carry volume quanta.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the question why geometry should not be quantized like angular momentum, and by the mini-black-hole argument; made concrete through the quantized tetrahedron.
concepts.notes: The chapter follows the heuristic presentation of Rovelli and Vidotto (2015).

concepts.name: Planck-scale localization limit
concepts.definition: Localizing a particle within a region L requires momentum spread at least hbar/L and hence energy at least hbar c/L; the corresponding horizon radius (about G E/c^4) equals L when L is about the Planck length, so a smaller region cannot be probed without forming a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the intuition behind LQG at the start of Section 49.6.
concepts.notes: The book writes the Schwarzschild radius as GM/c^2 (dropping the factor 2), acceptable at order-of-magnitude level.

concepts.name: tetrahedron area vectors and closure
concepts.definition: For a tetrahedron, the four outward face normals scaled by their face areas sum to zero; the volume follows from any three of them via V^2 = (2/9) L1 x L2 . L3.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a convenient classical description of a tetrahedron (Fig. 49.10a) that can then be quantized; proofs are Exercises 49.9-49.10.
concepts.notes: Closure is the discrete version of the divergence theorem applied to a constant vector field.

concepts.name: angular momentum algebra
concepts.definition: [L^i, L^j] = i hbar epsilon^{ijk} L^k; it implies L^2 eigenvalues hbar^2 j(j+1) with j half-integer or integer, and that only L^2 and one component can be sharp simultaneously.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the textbook example of how commutation relations generate quantization, then transplanted to geometry.

concepts.name: quantum of area
concepts.definition: If face-area vectors obey angular-momentum-like commutators with a Planck-scale constant l0^2, each face area takes discrete values l0^2 sqrt(j(j+1)), and the different Cartesian components of face normals cannot all be known, so geometry is fuzzy at the Planck scale.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced by direct analogy with angular momentum after postulating eqn 49.43.

concepts.name: quantum of volume
concepts.definition: Because the volume operator commutes with the four face-area operators and the closure constraint, tetrahedron states can be labelled |j1 j2 j3 j4 v>, and volume changes only in discrete steps.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows immediately from the quantized tetrahedron discussion.

concepts.name: spin network graph
concepts.definition: The graph dual to a mesh of quantum cells: nodes represent chunks of volume, links represent shared faces carrying area quanta, and closed paths through the graph are the loops that name the theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 49.10(b) shows a planar graph of triangles and nodes, described as analogous to lines of force.
concepts.notes: The term spin network is not used in the book.

concepts.name: de Sitter spacetime
concepts.definition: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with positive cosmological constant. It can be realized as a one-sheeted hyperboloid of radius alpha in five-dimensional Minkowski space, has topology R x S^3 (spatial 3-spheres that shrink to radius alpha and re-expand), and has constant positive curvature K = 1/alpha^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapters 15 and 18 as the stepping stone to AdS, with an embedding picture (Fig. 49.11).

concepts.name: anti-de Sitter spacetime
concepts.definition: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with negative cosmological constant; it is the hyperboloid -T^2 - U^2 + X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = -alpha^2 in a flat space with two time directions, has constant negative curvature R_{mu nu alpha beta} = -alpha^-2 (g g - g g), and possesses a timelike conformal boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a way to put gravity in a box, obtained from de Sitter by flipping the sign of alpha^2 and making one more embedding direction timelike (Fig. 49.12).

concepts.name: hyperboloid embedding
aliases: embedding a spacetime in higher-dimensional flat space
concepts.definition: Realizing a curved spacetime as a quadric surface in a higher-dimensional flat space and obtaining its metric by eliminating one embedding coordinate using the surface equation; maximally symmetric spaces are exactly such quadrics.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied through the Appendix D routine to both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter.
concepts.notes: The printed eqns 49.47 and 49.52 omit dX^mu dX^nu.

concepts.name: maximally symmetric spacetime
concepts.definition: A space with the largest possible number of independent symmetries, n(n+1)/2 in n dimensions, as many as flat space. Its Riemann tensor is fixed entirely by the metric and a single constant curvature K (formula below). Spheres, de Sitter and anti-de Sitter are examples.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain de Sitter's versatility in cosmological slicings and to link it to a sphere under T^2 -> -T^2.
concepts.notes: The book says 'same number of symmetries as Euclidean space' without giving the count.

concepts.name: constant-curvature Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: For a maximally symmetric space the full Riemann tensor is fixed by one constant: K = +1/alpha^2 for de Sitter and K = -1/alpha^2 for anti-de Sitter.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in margin notes 25 and 26 from Chapters 15-16.

concepts.name: closed timelike curves
concepts.definition: Future-directed timelike curves that return to their starting event, allowing an observer to meet their own past; they violate causality and are usually regarded as unphysical.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out for the AdS hyperboloid, where global time runs around a circle in the (T, U) plane.

concepts.name: universal covering of AdS
concepts.definition: Removing AdS's closed timelike curves by letting the periodic global time coordinate run over the whole real line, which changes the topology from S^1 x R^3 to R^4 while leaving the local geometry untouched.
concepts.how_introduced: Described informally as cutting the tube-shaped hyperboloid and unrolling it.

concepts.name: global AdS coordinates
concepts.definition: For AdS3 (alpha = 1), T = sqrt(1+r^2) cos t, U = sqrt(1+r^2) sin t, X = r cos theta, Y = r sin theta, giving ds^2 = -(1+r^2) dt^2 + dr^2/(1+r^2) + r^2 dtheta^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the standard coordinates that make the unrolling explicit.

concepts.name: conformal compactification
concepts.definition: Rewriting a metric as an overall positive factor times a simpler metric whose coordinates have finite range, so that infinity is brought to a finite coordinate location while light-cone structure is preserved.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 19 in Example 49.11 by substituting r = tan psi.

concepts.name: conformal boundary of AdS
concepts.definition: The timelike surface at conformal latitude psi = pi/2 (r -> infinity), or w = 0 in Poincare coordinates, which light can reach in finite coordinate time and which is itself a flat spacetime of one lower dimension; AdS behaves like a box with reflecting walls.
concepts.how_introduced: Discovered by noting that the latitude-like coordinate only reaches the equator, then visualized in Poincare coordinates (Fig. 49.13a).

concepts.name: Poincare coordinates for AdS
concepts.definition: Coordinates in which AdS takes the form ds^2 = (-dt^2 + dx^2 + dw^2)/w^2, so each constant-w slice is conformal to Minkowski space and the boundary lies at w = 0; they cover only part of global AdS.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to examine the boundary, with a pointer to the Poincare half-plane line element met earlier and a derivation in Exercise 49.12.

concepts.name: holographic principle
concepts.definition: The proposal, associated with 't Hooft, that the physics of a gravitating region of d dimensions can be fully encoded by degrees of freedom on its (d-1)-dimensional boundary, as a hologram stores a 3D image on a 2D plate.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 23, with AdS given as the vivid example; the massive-particle example hints how bulk depth encodes energy.

concepts.name: AdS/CFT correspondence
concepts.definition: Maldacena's conjecture that certain quantum gravity (string) theories on (d+1)-dimensional AdS are exactly equivalent to conformal field theories without gravity living on the d-dimensional boundary; the radial bulk direction corresponds to energy scale in the boundary theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the text and margin note 24 as the reason AdS attracts interest; the w = b turning point is offered as a hint of energy-to-depth mapping.
concepts.notes: The margin note says it was first proposed for 'spin theory'; string theory is meant.

concepts.name: Lambda-CDM model
concepts.definition: The Big-Bang cosmological model with a cosmological constant (dark energy) and cold dark matter plus baryons and radiation, spatially flat to high precision, fitting CMB, supernova and nucleosynthesis data with Omega_B ~ 0.05, Omega_M ~ 0.26, Omega_Lambda ~ 0.69 and age 13.80 Gyr.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as the answer to which model describes our Universe, unpacked term by term, then told as a history and critically assessed.

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: Nearly isotropic blackbody radiation at 2.725 K released when the Universe became transparent about 380,000 years after the Big Bang; its 10^-5 temperature fluctuations encode cosmological parameters through acoustic oscillations.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented through the COBE, WMAP and Planck missions as the data driving precision cosmology.

concepts.name: precision cosmology
concepts.definition: The modern era in which cosmological parameters are measured to per-cent or better accuracy by independent methods, replacing the qualitative debates of the mid twentieth century.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with 1950s arguments about whether the Universe had a beginning.

concepts.name: density parameters
concepts.definition: Ratios of the densities of each cosmic component to the critical density needed for spatial flatness; their sum Omega_0 is measured to be 0.999(2).
concepts.how_introduced: Used to quantify the baryon, dark matter and dark energy budget of Lambda-CDM.
concepts.notes: The text labels the CDM share Omega_M; in most references Omega_M includes baryons (about 0.31) and Omega_c ~ 0.26 is the CDM share.

concepts.name: dark energy
concepts.definition: The smooth component responsible for the present accelerating expansion, consistent with a cosmological constant; it is uniform in space, has very low density, but dominates the energy budget at about 69 per cent.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the Lambda of Lambda-CDM and the filler needed to make Omega_0 equal one; its origin is called even more mysterious than dark matter.

concepts.name: vacuum energy problem
concepts.definition: Naive estimates of the quantum vacuum energy density, which would act as a cosmological constant, exceed the observed dark-energy density by enormous factors, so why Lambda is so small is unexplained.
concepts.how_introduced: Attributed to Zel'dovich (1968), quoted as a mismatch of about fifty orders of magnitude.
concepts.notes: Other estimates quote up to 120 orders of magnitude depending on the cutoff.

concepts.name: inflation
concepts.definition: An early phase of near-exponential expansion driven by a scalar field's potential energy, which flattens the Universe, seeds nearly scale-invariant fluctuations and gravitational waves, and ends by converting field energy into particles (reheating).
concepts.how_introduced: Placed around 10^-32 s in the cosmic timeline, with a pointer to Chapter 41, and listed as poorly understood.

concepts.name: baryogenesis
concepts.definition: The unexplained process that left a small excess of baryons over antibaryons (a few per billion photons) before mutual annihilation; it requires baryon-number, C and CP violation out of equilibrium.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 35 in the cosmic timeline.

concepts.name: Big-Bang nucleosynthesis
concepts.definition: Formation of the light nuclei (mostly helium-4, with deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7) during the first minutes; its predicted abundances depend on the baryon density and cross-check the CMB.
concepts.how_introduced: In the cosmic timeline and as one of two independent confirmations of Lambda-CDM parameters.
concepts.notes: The printed list has '3Li', presumably helium-3 was meant.

concepts.name: recombination and last scattering
concepts.definition: The epoch about 380,000 years after the Big Bang when nuclei captured electrons into neutral atoms, photons stopped scattering, and the Universe became transparent, releasing the CMB.
concepts.how_introduced: Part of the cosmic timeline.

concepts.name: Hubble tension
concepts.definition: The disagreement between values of the Hubble constant inferred from the early Universe (about 67 km/s/Mpc) and measured locally (about 74 km/s/Mpc), unresolved at the time of writing.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among the wrinkles in Lambda-CDM.

concepts.name: Einstein-de Sitter (matter-dominated) era
concepts.definition: The stretch of cosmic history after radiation stops dominating, when cold pressureless matter (baryons plus dark matter) governs the expansion. It is well approximated by the flat, matter-only Einstein-de Sitter model, until the cosmological constant takes over about 5 Gyr ago.
concepts.how_introduced: Placed in the Lambda-CDM timeline right after recombination. A margin note explains matter domination: matter density falls as a^-3 but radiation as a^-4. The text links back to the model called Universe 3 in Chapter 18.

key_equations.name: Gravity as a time rescaling (Coleman)
key_equations.latex: \hat U = e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar} \to e^{-i\hat H(1+V)t/\hbar}
key_equations.meaning: Adding the potential energy HV to the rest-energy Hamiltonian is the same as stretching the time parameter by (1+V), which is gravitational time dilation.
key_equations.symbols: H Hamiltonian (rest energy m, c = 1); V = gh gravitational potential; t time

key_equations.name: Schrodinger equation on the 2D well
key_equations.meaning: Free-particle equation inside a well of length L in x with y periodic.
key_equations.symbols: psi wavefunction; m mass; E energy

key_equations.name: Eigenfunctions
key_equations.meaning: Separable solutions: standing wave in x times a periodic function around the compact circle.
key_equations.symbols: n, l integers; a compactification radius; L well length

key_equations.name: Energy levels with a compact dimension
key_equations.meaning: l = 0 gives the usual 1D levels; any excitation around the circle costs at least hbar^2/(2ma^2), huge when a is tiny.
key_equations.symbols: as above

key_equations.name: Constants in Planck units
key_equations.meaning: Dimensional relations that, solved for the three scales, give the Planck units.
key_equations.symbols: l_P, t_P, m_P Planck length, time, mass

key_equations.name: Planck units
key_equations.meaning: The natural scales where quantum mechanics and gravity meet.
key_equations.symbols: G Newton's constant; hbar reduced Planck constant; c speed of light

key_equations.name: Poisson equation, 3+1 dimensions
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian gravity in ordinary spacetime.
key_equations.symbols: Phi^(D) potential in D spacetime dimensions; rho mass density

key_equations.name: Poisson equation, D dimensions
key_equations.meaning: Same form with a dimension-dependent coupling; implies a force falling as 1/r^(d-1).
key_equations.symbols: G^(D) D-dimensional gravitational coupling; d = D - 1

key_equations.name: Planck length in D dimensions
key_equations.meaning: The fundamental length when the gravitational coupling is the higher-dimensional one.
key_equations.symbols: l_P^(D) D-dimensional Planck length

key_equations.name: Five-dimensional Poisson equation with a compact circle
key_equations.meaning: Mass spread uniformly around the circle has 5D density equal to the 4D density divided by the circumference.
key_equations.symbols: a radius of compact dimension

key_equations.name: Measured G from 5D gravity
key_equations.meaning: Observed gravity is weakened relative to the fundamental coupling by the size of the hidden dimension.
key_equations.symbols: l_c characteristic compact length

key_equations.name: General dilution of gravity
key_equations.meaning: The ratio of couplings equals the volume of the compact dimensions.
key_equations.symbols: V_c compact volume

key_equations.name: Point-particle action
key_equations.meaning: Action proportional to proper time along the world line; template for the string.
key_equations.symbols: m mass; tau world-line parameter; g metric

key_equations.name: Induced world-sheet metric
key_equations.meaning: Pull-back of the spacetime metric onto the world sheet.
key_equations.symbols: xi^1 = tau, xi^2 = sigma; X^mu embedding

key_equations.name: Dot and prime notation
key_equations.meaning: Shorthand for world-sheet derivatives.

key_equations.name: Induced metric as a matrix
key_equations.latex: \gamma_{\alpha\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} \dot X^2 & \dot X\cdot X' \\ \dot X\cdot X' & X'^2 \end{pmatrix}
key_equations.meaning: The world-sheet metric in terms of tangent vectors; its determinant is negative for a timelike sheet.
key_equations.symbols: dot products taken with eta_{mu nu}

key_equations.name: World-sheet area
key_equations.latex: A = \int d\tau\, d\sigma\sqrt{-\gamma},\qquad \gamma = \dot X^2 X'^2 - (\dot X\cdot X')^2
key_equations.meaning: Proper area of the world sheet, independent of parametrization.
key_equations.symbols: gamma determinant of gamma_{alpha beta}

key_equations.name: Nambu-Goto action
key_equations.latex: S = -T_0\int d\tau\, d\sigma\left[(\dot X\cdot X')^2 - \dot X^2 X'^2\right]^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: String action equals minus tension times world-sheet area. The printed version shows (X.X')^2 without the dot, and the same slip occurs in the determinant and eqn 49.19.
key_equations.symbols: T0 string tension

key_equations.name: String Lagrangian density
key_equations.meaning: Integrand of the Nambu-Goto action on the (tau, sigma) plane.

key_equations.name: Field Euler-Lagrange equation
key_equations.meaning: Recalled from Chapter 40 in margin note 11.
key_equations.symbols: phi scalar field

key_equations.name: Momentum-like variables and Euler-Lagrange for X^mu
key_equations.latex:
\mathcal P^
u_\mu =  rac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial X^\mu_{,
u}},\qquad  rac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial X^\mu} = (\mathcal P^
u_\mu)_{,
u}
key_equations.meaning: Each world-sheet direction nu = tau, sigma gets its own momentum current; X^mu does not appear undifferentiated, so the currents are conserved.
key_equations.symbols: nu world-sheet index; mu spacetime index

key_equations.name: World-sheet momenta
key_equations.latex: P^\tau_\mu = -\frac{T_0}{\sqrt{-\gamma}}\left[(\dot X\cdot X')X'_\mu - X'^2\dot X_\mu\right],\qquad P^\sigma_\mu = -\frac{T_0}{\sqrt{-\gamma}}\left[(\dot X\cdot X')\dot X_\mu - \dot X^2 X'_\mu\right]
key_equations.meaning: Derivatives of the Lagrangian density with respect to Xdot and X'. The book writes the prefactor as -T0/L; differentiating the square root actually gives -T0/sqrt(-gamma), equivalently T0^2/L.
key_equations.symbols: sqrt(-gamma) = [(Xdot.X')^2 - Xdot^2 X'^2]^(1/2)

key_equations.name: String equations of motion
key_equations.meaning: Conservation of world-sheet momentum currents; nonlinear in general.

key_equations.name: Static gauge derivatives
key_equations.meaning: With tau = t the time component of X is trivial.
key_equations.symbols: vec X spatial position of string point

key_equations.name: Arc length and unit tangent
key_equations.latex: ds = \left|\frac{d\vec X}{d\sigma}\right| d\sigma,\qquad \frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial s}\cdot\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial s} = 1
key_equations.meaning: Derivative with respect to arc length is a unit tangent to the string.
key_equations.symbols: s arc length

key_equations.name: Transverse velocity
key_equations.latex: \vec v_\perp = \frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial t} - \left(\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial t}\cdot\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial s}\right)\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial s}
key_equations.meaning: Velocity with its component along the string removed.

key_equations.name: Square-root argument in static gauge
key_equations.latex: \dot X^2 = -1 + \left(\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial t}\right)^2,\quad X'^2 = \left(\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial\sigma}\right)^2;\qquad (\dot X\cdot X')^2 - \dot X^2 X'^2 = \left(\frac{ds}{d\sigma}\right)^2(1 - v_\perp^2)
key_equations.meaning: The Nambu-Goto integrand depends only on the transverse speed and the stretching ds/dsigma.

key_equations.name: Static-gauge string action
key_equations.meaning: Each length element acts like a relativistic particle of mass T0 ds moving with transverse speed v_perp.

key_equations.name: Orthogonality gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Choose sigma lines so points move perpendicular to the string, making v_perp equal the full velocity.

key_equations.name: Momenta in static gauge
key_equations.latex: P^{\tau\mu} = T_0(1 - v_\perp^2)^{-1/2}\frac{ds}{d\sigma}\frac{\partial X^\mu}{\partial t},\qquad P^{\sigma\mu} = -T_0(1 - v_\perp^2)^{1/2}\frac{\partial X^\mu}{\partial s}
key_equations.meaning: Momentum density looks like a relativistic particle momentum; the sigma current is the tension force along the tangent. The text says these come from eqns 49.25; they are really eqns 49.23-49.24 evaluated in this gauge.

key_equations.name: Intermediate equation of motion
key_equations.meaning: Equation of motion before the final sigma choice; verified in Exercise 49.6.

key_equations.name: Energy-weighted sigma parametrization
key_equations.meaning: Sigma measures energy along the string, since energy per length is T0/sqrt(1 - v_perp^2).

key_equations.name: String wave equation
key_equations.meaning: In this gauge the string's spatial position obeys the linear 1D wave equation (with c = 1), subject to the gauge constraints.

key_equations.name: Supersymmetry operator
key_equations.meaning: The supersymmetry generator swaps bosons and fermions.
key_equations.symbols: Q supersymmetry generator

key_equations.name: Phase of a 3-geometry
key_equations.meaning: Each configuration of 3-space contributes with a phase set by its classical action.
key_equations.symbols: (3)C a spatial 3-geometry; S classical action

key_equations.name: Einstein-Hamilton-Jacobi equation
key_equations.meaning: Governs how surfaces of constant action move through superspace; equivalent in content to Einstein's equation.
key_equations.symbols: gamma_ij 3-metric; gamma its determinant; (3)R Ricci scalar of the 3-geometry

key_equations.name: Mini-black-hole estimate of the Planck length
key_equations.meaning: Localizing a particle below the Planck length would hide it behind its own horizon.
key_equations.symbols: L localization size; R horizon radius

key_equations.name: Angular momentum commutator
key_equations.meaning: The template quantization rule.

key_equations.name: Tetrahedron closure
key_equations.meaning: Area-weighted face normals of a closed tetrahedron sum to zero; the volume follows from three of them.
key_equations.symbols: L_a area vector of face a

key_equations.name: Quantized geometry commutator
key_equations.meaning: Postulate treating each face-area vector as an angular momentum with a Planck-scale area constant.
key_equations.symbols: l0 constant times Planck length

key_equations.name: Area spectrum
key_equations.meaning: Face areas come in discrete quanta.
key_equations.symbols: j_a spin-like quantum number of face a

key_equations.name: de Sitter hyperboloid
key_equations.latex: -T^2 + X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 + W^2 = \alpha^2,\qquad ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2 + dY^2 + dZ^2 + dW^2
key_equations.meaning: de Sitter spacetime as a one-sheeted hyperboloid in (4+1) Minkowski space.
key_equations.symbols: alpha de Sitter radius

key_equations.name: Induced de Sitter line element
key_equations.meaning: Result of eliminating W; indices run 0-3. The printed equation omits the differentials dX^mu dX^nu and reuses mu nu as dummy indices in the denominator.

key_equations.name: Constant-curvature Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: Maximal symmetry fixes curvature up to one constant.
key_equations.symbols: K sectional curvature

key_equations.name: AdS Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: AdS has constant negative curvature.

key_equations.name: AdS hyperboloid
key_equations.latex: -T^2 + X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 - U^2 = -\alpha^2,\qquad ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2 + dY^2 + dZ^2 - dU^2
key_equations.meaning: AdS as a hyperboloid in (3+2)-dimensional flat space with two timelike directions.
key_equations.symbols: U second timelike embedding coordinate

key_equations.name: Induced AdS line element
key_equations.meaning: Obtained from the de Sitter result by alpha^2 -> -alpha^2. The printed version omits the differentials.

key_equations.name: Global AdS3 coordinates and metric
key_equations.latex: T = \sqrt{1+r^2}\cos t,\ U = \sqrt{1+r^2}\sin t,\ X = r\cos\theta,\ Y = r\sin\theta;\qquad ds^2 = -(1+r^2)dt^2 + \frac{dr^2}{1+r^2} + r^2 d\theta^2
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates on the AdS3 hyperboloid (alpha = 1); t is periodic on the hyperboloid and unrolled in the covering space.

key_equations.name: Conformal AdS3 metric
key_equations.meaning: AdS is conformal to half of a static cylinder; psi only reaches pi/2, revealing a boundary.
key_equations.symbols: psi latitude-like coordinate

key_equations.name: Poincare AdS metric
key_equations.meaning: Constant-w slices are flat Minkowski space up to scale; boundary at w = 0.
key_equations.symbols: w radial Poincare coordinate

key_equations.name: Normalization of massive geodesic
key_equations.meaning: u.u = -1 for motion in the (t, w) plane of Poincare AdS; dots are proper-time derivatives.

key_equations.name: Conserved energy
key_equations.meaning: Time-translation Killing vector gives a conserved u_t; b is a constant length set by initial conditions. The reading copy loses the dot, printing t = w^2/b.
key_equations.symbols: b turning-point parameter

key_equations.name: Effective radial motion
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic plus potential energy (b/w)^2 is constant; the diverging potential turns massive particles back at w = b before the boundary.

key_equations.name: Lambda-CDM energy budget
key_equations.meaning: Measured composition of the Universe in units of the critical density.
key_equations.symbols: Omega_B baryons; Omega_M cold dark matter (as labelled in the text); Omega_Lambda dark energy

key_equations.name: Transverse speed squared (Exercise 49.4)
key_equations.latex: v_\perp^2 = \left(\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial t}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial s}\cdot\frac{\partial\vec X}{\partial t}\right)^2
key_equations.meaning: Pythagoras for the velocity split along and across the string.

key_equations.name: Cosmic string interior and exterior metrics (Exercises 49.7-49.8)
key_equations.latex: ds^2_{\rm in} = -dt^2 + r_0^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2) + dz^2,\qquad ds^2_{\rm out} = -dt^2 + r_0^2\left(\frac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta_m}d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2\right) + dz^2
key_equations.meaning: Interior is a spherical cap cross-section; exterior is locally flat but conical, with a circumference deficit.
key_equations.symbols: r0 constant radius; theta_m edge of string core

key_equations.name: Tetrahedron volume (Exercise 49.10)
key_equations.latex: V = \tfrac16|\vec a\times\vec b\cdot\vec c|,\qquad V^2 = \tfrac29|\vec L_1\times\vec L_2\cdot\vec L_3|
key_equations.meaning: Links the edge-vector and area-vector descriptions of a tetrahedron.
key_equations.symbols: a, b, c edge vectors from one vertex

key_equations.name: Poincare embedding of AdS3 (Exercise 49.12)
key_equations.meaning: Explicit map from Poincare coordinates to the AdS3 hyperboloid (T^2 - X^2) + (W^2 - Y^2) = 1.

figures.label: Fig. 49.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A square well stretched into two dimensions, with its y direction to be identified periodically.
figures.visual_description: Axes x (horizontal, marked 0 and L) and y (vertical). Two tall vertical walls stand at x = 0 and x = L. A thin horizontal line joins the walls at height 2 pi a; dotted arcs on each wall link the line at 2 pi a back down to the x-axis, indicating that y = 0 and y = 2 pi a are the same.
figures.what_it_teaches: How to model a hidden dimension: a well that is finite in x and periodic in y.

redesign.idea: Roll-up well: a flat 2D well that the learner can roll into a cylinder, with the energy ladder beside it splitting into n-levels and a far-off l-tower.
redesign.interaction: Slider for compact radius a (from comparable to L down to tiny); drag to roll the sheet into a tube; the energy-level plot shows l = 0 levels fixed while l >= 1 levels shoot upward as 1/a^2; hover a level to see its wavefunction on the cylinder.

figures.label: Fig. 49.1(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same well after rolling up y: a thin tube running from 0 to L.
figures.visual_description: A narrow horizontal cylinder drawn in outline, with elliptical end caps, running from a label 0 at the left to L at the right.
figures.what_it_teaches: At large scales the compactified space looks one-dimensional; the circle is only visible up close.

redesign.idea: Merged into the roll-up well demo as its end state, with a zoom control that makes the tube look like a line from far away.
redesign.interaction: Zoom slider shows the circle shrinking below pixel size as the viewer backs off.

figures.label: Fig. 49.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: An open string whose two ends are stuck on a two-dimensional brane.
figures.visual_description: A hand-drawn tilted rectangular sheet (hatched) in perspective with x, y, z axes at its upper right corner. On the sheet, a thick curved arc like a letter D bulges outward with two black dots at its endpoints lying on the sheet.
figures.what_it_teaches: Open string endpoints can be confined to a brane (Dirichlet boundary conditions) while the string body moves freely.

redesign.idea: Brane playground: an open string whose ends slide on a plane while the middle vibrates in and out of it.
redesign.interaction: Toggle each endpoint between free (Neumann) and brane-fixed (Dirichlet); pluck the string and watch modes; change brane dimension from a line to a plane.

figures.label: Fig. 49.3(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A particle decaying into two, drawn as a Feynman vertex.
figures.visual_description: A single line with an arrow enters from the left and splits at a sharp point into two outgoing arrowed lines to upper right and lower right, forming a Y shape.
figures.what_it_teaches: In point-particle field theory the interaction happens at one spacetime point, the source of short-distance divergences.

redesign.idea: Vertex versus trousers: side-by-side Y vertex and string pair-of-pants; zooming in on the vertex never smooths it, zooming in on the string junction always does.
redesign.interaction: Shared zoom slider; a probe circle shows how 'where the split happens' depends on the observer's time slicing for the string but is sharp for the point.

figures.label: Fig. 49.3(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same decay in string theory: one tube smoothly branching into two.
figures.visual_description: A shaded tube enters from the left and smoothly forks into two tubes heading upper right and lower right, like a pair of trousers lying on its side, with arrows beside the tubes showing direction of travel.
figures.what_it_teaches: Closed-string interactions are smeared over a smooth surface with no special point.

redesign.idea: Combined with Fig. 49.3(a) in the vertex versus trousers demo, adding a sweeping time slice that shows one loop becoming two.
redesign.interaction: Tilt the slicing plane to show that different observers disagree on where the split happens.

figures.label: Fig. 49.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: World sheets swept out by (a) an open string and (b) a closed string.
figures.visual_description: Axes at left with t up, y right and x out of page. Panel (a): a wavy vertical ribbon, a sheet with two free edges running upward in t. Panel (b): a vertical tube with an elliptical opening at the top, bulging and pinching as it rises.
figures.what_it_teaches: A string moving in time traces a 2D surface: a strip for open strings, a tube for closed ones.

redesign.idea: World-sheet builder: animate a string in the xy-plane and stack its snapshots up the t axis to grow the world sheet live.
redesign.interaction: Choose open or closed, draw an initial shape, press play; rotate the growing surface; scrub a time slider to highlight the current snapshot.

figures.label: Fig. 49.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Static gauge: a constant-time plane slices the world sheet, and the cut is the string at that time.
figures.visual_description: A t axis arrow on the left. A horizontal parallelogram labelled t = const cuts through a wavy vertical sheet labelled WORLDSHEET; the part of the sheet below the plane is shown dashed or hatched, and the intersection curve is where the plane meets the sheet.
figures.what_it_teaches: Choosing tau = t identifies constant-parameter lines on the world sheet with the string as seen at one instant.

redesign.idea: Slice-and-label: a world sheet with a movable t = const plane; the intersection curve is extracted and shown flat, with sigma tick marks that can be redistributed.
redesign.interaction: Drag the plane up and down; switch sigma labelling between uniform parameter, arc length, and energy-weighted; watch v_perp arrows on the extracted string.

figures.label: Fig. 49.6(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: High-temperature potential: a single bowl with its minimum at zero field.
figures.visual_description: Axes U(phi) vertical and phi horizontal; a U-shaped parabola-like curve with its minimum at the origin.
figures.what_it_teaches: Before the transition the symmetric state phi = 0 is the vacuum.

redesign.idea: Cooling potential: one curve that morphs from single well to double well as temperature drops, with a ball that must choose a side.
redesign.interaction: Temperature slider reshapes U(phi); add noise to see random choices of the minimum; link to a 1D lattice of such balls that forms domains.

figures.label: Fig. 49.6(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Low-temperature broken-symmetry potential: two minima either side of a local maximum at zero.
figures.visual_description: Axes U(phi) and phi; a W-shaped double-well curve, dipping below the axis to two symmetric minima and rising to a small local maximum at phi = 0.
figures.what_it_teaches: Below the transition the vacuum is at +phi0 or -phi0, so the symmetry is broken by the choice.

redesign.idea: End state of the cooling potential demo.

figures.label: Fig. 49.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Field profile across a domain wall joining the -phi0 and +phi0 vacua.
figures.visual_description: Axes phi(x) vertical and x horizontal, with tick marks phi0 and -phi0. The curve sits flat at -phi0 on the left, rises steeply in an S-shaped (tanh-like) step, and levels off at phi0 on the right. A double-headed arrow below the step marks the width of the wall.
figures.what_it_teaches: Mismatched vacua must be joined by a region of non-vacuum field that carries energy: a topological defect.

redesign.idea: Kink energy lab: the learner drags the wall width and sees gradient energy and potential energy trade off, with the minimum-energy width highlighted.
redesign.interaction: Width slider; plots of gradient-energy density, potential-energy density and total; try to remove the kink by continuous deformation and see the endpoints stay pinned.

figures.label: Fig. 49.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: The broken-symmetry potential for a complex field, likened to the base of a wine bottle, with its ring of minima.
figures.visual_description: Three hand-drawn panels. (a) A wine bottle labelled CHATEAU LANDAU, with an arrow pointing out of its base. (b) The upturned punt of the bottle drawn as a bowl whose floor rises to a central hump, with dashed contour circles: the Mexican-hat surface. (c) Axes phi1 and phi2 with a dotted circle of minima and a small open marker on the circle indicating one chosen vacuum.
figures.what_it_teaches: For a complex field the vacua form a circle labelled by phase; choosing a ground state means picking one point on it.

redesign.idea: Mexican hat with a marble: a rotatable 3D hat surface with a marble that settles into the rim, linked to a phase dial showing theta0.
redesign.interaction: Drag the marble; lower the temperature to raise the central hump; rotate the hat; watch the phase dial and the (Re psi, Im psi) plane update.

figures.label: Fig. 49.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: A vortex in two dimensions: the field's phase, drawn as arrows, turns through one full circle as you go around the centre.
figures.visual_description: A 5 by 5 grid of short arrows. The arrows point radially outward from the middle of the grid (up along the top row, left along the left column, down along the bottom row, right along the right column, diagonally at the corners), a hedgehog-like pattern. Following the arrows once around the centre, their direction rotates through 360 degrees; the centre point has no well-defined direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: A complex field can wind its phase around a point; continuity then forces a singular core, the seed of a cosmic string.

redesign.idea: Winding number explorer: a phase-arrow field on a grid where the learner walks a loop and counts how many times the arrow turns; then extrude in z to build a string.
redesign.interaction: Place vortices and antivortices by clicking; drag a loop to read its winding number; try to smooth a vortex away; press extrude to stack slices into a 3D line defect.

figures.label: Fig. 49.10(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A tetrahedron described by four vectors normal to its faces, one per face.
figures.visual_description: A shaded tetrahedron (one face hatched, one stippled) with four arrows labelled L1 to L4 emerging perpendicular to its faces: L1 down from the bottom face, L2 to the left, L3 to the upper right, L4 up.
figures.what_it_teaches: A chunk of space can be encoded by area vectors that sum to zero, which can then be promoted to quantum operators.
